title: Why did we invent vampires?
subject: mythologie
description: Before it was an aristocrat in a cape, the vampire was a neighbor who died too soon and was blamed for taking his family with him. The story of a fear that found a name.
author: angela-bouma

hero.hook: Death is scary. Not being able to explain it is scarier.

blocks.text: In **1645**, a Greek scholar living in Rome, [[Leo Allatius]], described a creature feared by the villagers of his homeland: the [[vrykolakas]]. A dead man who walks by night and comes back to torment his own family, because he was buried without the last rites. Only fire can destroy him.

For two centuries, epidemics and unexplained deaths within the same household kept the belief alive. Every new body buried without the proper rites risked becoming another one. How did this village panic turn into the vampire in evening dress of novels and films?

sections.title: The dead man who asked for his shoes

blocks.text: In **1725**, in the Serbian village of Kisiljevo, then under Austrian administration, a peasant named [[Petar Blagojevic]] died. Within days, nine neighbors died in turn. All of them, in their final hours, accused him of coming to smother them at night. His widow said he had come back to ask her for his shoes, and then she left the village.

blocks.caption: Vampire, by Edvard Munch (1895). Before painters and novelists, the vampire was a village affair.

blocks.text: The villagers dug up the body. They found it strangely intact: fresh skin, blood at the mouth, hair and nails that seemed to have grown. Proof enough. They drove a stake through his heart and burned the remains. An Austrian official watched the scene and wrote a report. The word "vampire" spread through the newspapers of Europe.

What the villagers took for supernatural signs were the ordinary effects of decay. Gases produced by bacteria bloat the abdomen and the face, and force a dark fluid out of the mouth and nose that looks disturbingly like blood. The skin shrinks back and exposes the roots of the nails and hair, which seem longer.

In nineteenth-century New England, a different fear took the same shape. [[Tuberculosis]], then called "consumption," made its victims waste away and cough for months. Contagious, it passed from one member of a family to the next. Seen from outside, a dead relative seemed to be coming back to drain the life from the survivors, one after another. It does not explain the older Balkan tradition: the two are separate, parallel beliefs, born in different times and places, but answering the same anxiety.

blocks.caption: Mercy Brown's grave in Exeter, Rhode Island, still visited today.

blocks.text: In **1892**, in Exeter, Rhode Island, [[Mercy Brown]] died of tuberculosis at 19, after her mother and sister. When her brother Edwin fell ill in turn, the neighbors exhumed all three bodies. Mercy's, buried in the depths of winter, was well preserved, and her heart still held blood. They burned it and gave the ashes to Edwin to drink, as a cure. He died two months later.
The vrykolakas is not unique to Greece. Ancient Mesopotamia had its own blood-drinking demons, Russia its *upyr*, and China its *jiangshi*, a stiff corpse that hops along with its arms outstretched.

In **1819**, a young English doctor, [[John Polidori]], published *The Vampyre*, the first sustained prose vampire story in English. The idea was born three years earlier, during the famous rainy summer on Lake Geneva when Mary Shelley dreamed up *Frankenstein*. His character, **Lord Ruthven**, has nothing left of the peasant risen from his grave: he is rich, mysterious, seductive, and hunts in the drawing rooms of London.

blocks.caption: The first edition of Dracula (1897), bound in yellow cloth and lettered in red.

blocks.text: The story was reprinted, translated and adapted for the stage. The society vampire caught on among Gothic writers. In **1897**, [[Bram Stoker]] published *Dracula* and fixed the model for a century: the count, the castle, the fangs, the garlic and the crucifixes. Almost everything the cinema would make of it is already there.
Stoker never set foot in Transylvania. He wrote *Dracula* from travel guides and the books of the public library in Whitby, the small English town where the count comes ashore in the novel.

Vampire traditions are not really about the supernatural. Before science could explain decay, contagion or sudden death, a community needed some way to make sense of what it saw. A returning corpse gives fear a shape and a name. And a culprit that can be burned.

events.title: Dracula
events.detail: Bram Stoker fixes the modern model.

blocks.text: The same mechanism produces the Greek vrykolakas, the Slavic *upyr*, the Chinese *jiangshi*: each one is a local answer to the same unanswered question. Werewolf legends follow the same pattern and fill the same gap, with transformation instead of blood.
Facing the same fears, every culture tells some version of the same story. A monster is easier to live with than an unanswered question.
